title: Psychoactive Plants Shaped Andean Civilization, Not Just Inca Beer
dek: Archaeologists have detected DMT and vilca in bone tubes, snuff trays and ceramic cups from Peru and Bolivia, suggesting hallucinogens were shared religious infrastructure across pre-Inca complex societies — while the Inca turned to drinking chicha beer.
why: The archaeology half has specific sites, artifacts and chemical evidence, and is dense with information; the education policy forum half is more framework-level and you can listen only for the conclusions.
who: Readers interested in archaeology, the history of hallucinogens, or ancient trade networks; and practitioners focused on global education policy implementation, implementation science and randomized trial methodology.
skip: The journal and news briefs around 17:13 can be skipped; they are unrelated to the two themes.

points.h: Two independent shifts opened up a forbidden research zone
points.body: Why was hallucinogen research taboo for so long, and why is it now a golden age for archaeology? Andrew Lawler gives two unrelated reasons. One is technology: over the past decade the tools for detecting residues on ancient pottery have advanced dramatically, able to identify dozens or even hundreds of molecules. The other is culture: drugs were once seen as addictive, abused substances, but now hallucinogens are having a revival in psychotherapy and PTSD treatment, putting them back on the research agenda. Only the combination of these two things has let archaeologists dare to touch this ‘largely unknown territory’.

points.h: The bigger the society, the less it could hold hallucinogens
points.body: Lawler lays out the Andean timeline: the earliest urban culture appeared on the coast around 2500 BC, followed by Chavín around 1500 to 500 BC, then regional powers such as Moche and Nazca at the turn of the Common Era, and around AD 600-1100 the two true proto-empires, Wari and Tiwanaku. The key judgment is: the larger and more complex the society, the harder it became to integrate hallucinogens into religious, social and political systems. By the Inca around AD 1200, they simply turned to drinking chicha beer, and interest in hallucinogens declined.

points.h: Chavín's underground tunnels were a sound-and-light show
points.body: Chavín de Huántar was not a political state but a place where pilgrims shared a belief system; it appeared around 1500 BC and lasted at least a thousand years. What really changed the picture was new residue analysis: researchers detected vilca and DMT in a set of bone tubes — bone tubes traditionally used to blow the drug into the noses of ritual participants. Rituals mostly took place in a network of underground tunnels, with decorated conch-shell trumpets and polished stones that reflected daylight from above. Sound, light and hallucinogens, led by priests, served both religious and political functions.

points.h: Cups shaped like cactus, but no mescaline detected
points.body: After Chavín, many ‘copycat’ sites appeared in the central Andes. At Catala, which Michelle Young is excavating, cups shaped like the San Pedro cactus were found in ritual spaces — fairly strong evidence of use. But researchers could not directly detect mescaline, because it may have degraded. The next step is to understand the compounds they can analyze; if they can figure out how mescaline degrades over time, it may be possible to piece together the fragments and prove the cups really held it. The technology is still getting better.

points.h: Llama caravans carried Amazonian drugs up to the highlands
points.body: Juan Caprillis found a set of wooden snuff trays in Bolivia, one of them made in the Amazon but placed in an extremely high, extremely remote cave. This shows a trade network existed: people brought hallucinogenic substances and other goods from the Amazon and from other parts of the Andes. Llamas became the core domesticated animal, helping early societies transport Amazonian macaw feathers, the ingredients for iawasa, and textiles from the coast to the central region. Lawler compares it to the Silk Road of Eurasia — a complex network spanning long distances.

points.h: Half of adult men in northern Chile were using vilca
points.body: At sites in northern Chile far from the Tiwanaku center in Bolivia, archaeologists found an enormous number of wooden snuff boards. How many? It looks like at least one in every two adult men was using them. These snuff boards were often buried with their owners' remains. This was an extremely widespread hallucinogen tradition, extending over a thousand miles and in multiple directions. Although the religious meaning cannot be fully grasped, implements unearthed across such vast distances are ‘remarkably similar’, indicating shared practices behind them.

points.h: Wari spiked beer with vilca; Tiwanaku snorted it straight
points.body: Two neighboring societies of the same period used it in completely different ways. Wari clearly drank large amounts of chicha beer, but new residue analysis and the discovery of vilca seeds indicate they mixed vilca into the beer — mixed into beer the effect is milder, less intense, possibly exactly what Wari preferred. Next door, Tiwanaku used wooden snuff boards to inhale the strong substance. The two societies existed almost simultaneously; Wari was more warlike and expanded an empire, while Tiwanaku has no evidence of an army and seems to have spread its culture in a more peaceful way.

points.h: Knowing what works is not knowing how to deliver it
points.body: Nome Angrist points out that the problem in global education is not a lack of evidence: structured pedagogy (giving teachers lesson structure, teacher guides and ongoing coaching) and ‘teaching at the right level’ (no one-size-fits-all curriculum; assess first, then teach to the child's actual level) both have substantial evidence behind them. The real gap is implementation science. Take a question that sounds simple but is crucial: where does this go in the school calendar? Does it replace math and language classes, or is it a separate remedial class? A large body of randomized trial evidence simply does not answer this question. Likewise, tutoring works, but how do you make it cheap enough for government systems to scale? Research often tests a ‘gold-plated’ expensive version.

points.h: Education should learn from tech's AB testing
points.body: Angrist argues methodology also needs to change. Traditional randomized controlled trials are the gold standard, but they are often one-off, slow, do not update over time, and are not run many times in quick succession. She advocates borrowing from the tech industry's AB testing: still randomized, still able to draw causal conclusions, but done fast, done frequently, and more embedded in the implementation system itself. This can answer not only ‘does it work’ but also ‘for whom, and where’, forming a continuously running learning engine to cope with the enormous heterogeneity of global education across regions and between urban and rural areas.

points.h: What evidence policymakers actually believe is unstudied
points.body: Angrist lists ‘the leap from evidence to policy practice’ itself as something that needs to be studied, rather than an afterthought. She lists a string of unanswered questions: do policymakers respond to local evidence or global evidence? Causal evidence or descriptive evidence? Numbers or words? She also mentions some preliminary evidence showing that many well-intentioned policies never actually get implemented, even when the policy itself is correct. Moreover, education is harder than health care: the biological mechanisms of medicine are more consistent across people and countries, whereas education is essentially social, and social structures, government structures and cultural structures are more complex, making implementation science all the more necessary.

points.h: Seventy percent of children in low- and middle-income countries are in ‘learning poverty’
points.body: Why write this policy forum article now? Angrist says the field is at a moment of momentum: academia has recognized the scale of the learning crisis. New global indicators show 70% of children in low- and middle-income countries are in learning poverty. At the same time, a lot of energy is going into research on implementation science and scaling problems. She hopes that in the coming decades considerable progress can be made on these kinds of implementation questions.
